line: d4 c5 e4 cxd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Qa4
teaches: Bringing the queen out early is only bad when she has to move again. Look for the square where the move that chases her has already been made — from there she is out, doing something, and the tempo the opponent expected to win is not available.
explains: The knight has come to c6 hitting the queen, and instead of retreating she steps sideways to a4, where she hits that same knight back and eyes the pawn on a7. She also holds the pawns on c2 and e4 from there. The move that was supposed to gain time has instead put the knight on a square where it is the piece being asked questions.

line: d4 c5 e4 cxd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Qa4 g6 Bd2 Bg7 c3
teaches: When your queen is out and slightly exposed, the pawn move that covers the squares an enemy piece would use to attack her is worth more than another developing move. Count where the attack could come from, then take those squares away — a queen nobody can hit is simply a developed piece.
explains: The pawn goes to c3 covering b4 and d4, which are the two squares a bishop or knight would use to come at the queen with tempo. It also blunts the fianchettoed bishop's diagonal. Nothing is developed by the move and the position becomes much harder to play against, because the loose piece stops being loose.

line: d4 c5 e4 cxd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Qa4 g6 Bd2 Bg7 c3 Nf6 Bf4
teaches: When a bishop lands on a square the opponent can challenge by shuffling a knight, the position is offering a repetition. Taking it is a legitimate result and refusing it is a decision — but decide, rather than drifting into the same squares three times without noticing what you agreed to.
explains: The bishop has come to f4 covering the dark squares in the middle. Black can step the knight back and invite the bishop to return, or castle and get on with the game. Both are playable and they lead to completely different results, so this is the moment to know which one you want.
